content.overview: A specialist differential should compare multiple plausible explanations across plant-health domains and update as new evidence arrives. The goal is not to name the first familiar disorder but to identify which evidence most strongly separates competing causes.

vocabulary.definition: An observation or test whose possible results meaningfully separate competing hypotheses.
Updated confidence in a hypothesis after considering new evidence; used here qualitatively rather than as a required numeric probability.
A different cause that can produce similar visible symptoms or crop responses.

sections.title: Build across domains
sections.body: Include biotic disease, arthropod damage, nutrient/root-zone, environmental, irrigation/process and genetic/developmental explanations when the observations plausibly support them.

sections.title: Track supporting and conflicting evidence
sections.body: A strong differential records what each hypothesis explains and what it fails to explain. Confidence should decrease when high-quality evidence conflicts with the hypothesis.

sections.title: Use asymptomatic infection as a reminder about test limits
sections.body: HLVd demonstrates why visible appearance may not reliably exclude disease. Diagnostic confidence must match the biology and sensitivity of the evidence available.

workedExamples: Stunting with leaf discoloration may keep nutrient/root-zone stress, chronic pest feeding and HLVd in the differential until spatial pattern, roots, pest evidence and appropriate testing separate them.
commonMistakes: Treating one plausible mechanism as the only mechanism.
Ignoring evidence because it complicates the preferred answer.
content.practicalApplication: Create a differential matrix with at least four hypotheses, supporting evidence, conflicting evidence, consequence if wrong and the next discriminating observation/test.
content.summary: A specialist differential stays broad enough to prevent premature closure and narrow enough to drive the next useful evidence.
